script.opening: "Afternoon doc. My voice has gone all husky and gravelly — been weeks now. I'm a publican and I smoke, so it's probably just a smoker's throat, or a cold that never quite went. Could you give me a throat spray or some antibiotics to clear it? I can't be doing without my voice behind the bar. It's nothing to worry about, surely — just need it to settle."

facts.text: About six weeks; slowly getting worse, not better. Started after a cold, but the cold went. Husky all day, not just in the morning.

Feeling of "something stuck" on the right side of your throat. An ache in your right ear, especially when swallowing — "but the ear's not blocked or anything". Food goes down fine; no choking. No coughing blood.

facts.topic: Neck — only if asked about lumps
facts.text: "Funny you should ask — there's a little lump here (right side of the neck, below the jaw). Noticed it shaving a couple of weeks ago. Doesn't hurt."
No noisy breathing, no breathlessness at rest. Belt "a notch looser" — maybe half a stone in two months.
40 a day since 16. "I run a pub — I have a few every night," about 50–60 units a week.
Nothing diagnosed. No regular medicines. No allergies.
63, runs a pub with wife Denise. Two grown-up children.
Your best mate from the darts team had throat cancer and "ended up with a hole in his neck". You have avoided thinking about it. Say this only if asked what you are worried about.

Jovial, minimising, keen to get a spray. If the doctor asks good questions you answer honestly, including the lump. If they explain a hoarse voice for this long needs an urgent specialist look, go quiet: "You're thinking cancer, aren't you?" Respond well to honesty and to hearing that early treatment works well. If smoking is raised as a lecture, get defensive; if it is offered as support, show interest.

ice.ideas: "It's a smoker's throat, or a cold that never cleared."
ice.concerns: Your voice for work. Underneath (only if asked): your mate's throat cancer.
ice.expectations: "A spray or antibiotics." You will accept an urgent referral if you are told honestly why.

cues: "It's nothing to worry about, surely." — say in the opening.
"My ear aches when I swallow." — say if asked about other symptoms.
"There's a little lump here." — say only if asked about lumps.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that PERSISTENT (in practice >3 weeks) progressive HOARSENESS at 45 or over — made more worrying by smoking and heavy alcohol — is a red flag for LARYNGEAL/head-and-neck cancer — NOT "a smoker’s throat" or a lingering cold — and does NOT just give a throat spray/antibiotics without assessment

Acts on NICE NG12: makes a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer (NG12: consider for persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained neck lump at 45+; he has both), with the associated head-and-neck features included in the referral

Elicits and weights the ASSOCIATED red flags by directed history/examination: a NECK LUMP, unilateral referred otalgia (with a normal ear), globus/throat discomfort, dysphagia/odynophagia, sore throat — and the combined smoking + heavy-alcohol risk

Arranges a prompt face-to-face examination (throat/oral cavity, neck/lymph nodes, ears — not possible on video) without letting it delay the referral, and recognises an unexplained persistent NECK LUMP as itself warranting urgent referral

Reassures accurately (early laryngeal/head-and-neck cancer is very treatable, often voice-preserving — urgent referral is precautionary) and addresses SMOKING and ALCOHOL supportively as the major modifiable risks
Gently challenges the "just a smoker’s throat" minimisation and surfaces the noticed lump and underlying cancer fear, rather than colluding with the spray/antibiotic request
Balances honesty (this needs urgent checking) with genuine reassurance and concern for his livelihood/voice, so he accepts the referral; addresses smoking/alcohol without a lecture that alienates

Safety-nets and follows up: the urgent suspected cancer pathway referral and what to expect (nasendoscopy/ENT assessment), reassurance, smoking/alcohol support, what to report (worsening, the lump enlarging, swallowing/breathing trouble), and a follow-up — referring the likely cancer, not spraying it

worked.txt: "I’m glad you came. Here’s the important rule though: a voice that stays husky for more than about three weeks — especially over the age of 45, and more so in someone who smokes and drinks — we never just put down to a smoker’s throat or an old cold. It needs looking at properly, because occasionally a persistent hoarse voice is the first sign of something in the voice box we’d want to catch early. So a spray isn’t the answer here."

"Can I ask a few things? Any ache in your throat or one ear? Any trouble swallowing? And — have you noticed any lumps in your neck? … You have, on one side. Thank you for telling me — that’s important, and it’s exactly why I want this checked rather than treated blind."

"I want to be straight with you: a husky voice this long, with that neck lump, in a smoker, is something I need to refer urgently to rule out a cancer of the voice box or throat. Before that frightens you — the genuinely reassuring part is that caught early, these are very treatable, often keeping your voice. Getting seen now is how we keep it simple."

worked.lbl: The urgent suspected cancer pathway referral
worked.txt: "So I’m referring you urgently to the ear-nose-throat specialists on the suspected cancer pathway — usually seen within about two weeks. I’d also like to see you in person to check your neck and throat, but that won’t hold up the referral. They’ll look at your voice box with a tiny camera and check your neck. That’s the right, safe step, and it’s why antibiotics wouldn’t have done anything."

"I’m not going to lecture you behind your own bar — but the smoking and the drink are the two biggest things behind throat problems, and cutting them is the best thing you could do for your voice AND your recovery. When you’re ready, I’ll help you with both, properly. No judgement."

"If your swallowing gets worse, the lump grows, or you get any trouble breathing, tell us sooner. I’ll get the urgent referral done and follow it up with you. You came in for a spray for your voice; what you actually needed was to get this looked at properly — and most likely sorted while it’s early."

f.learning: Hoarseness persisting beyond ~3 weeks — especially progressive and in a smoker over 45 — is a red flag for laryngeal/head-and-neck cancer, NOT "a smoker’s throat" or a lingering cold, so NICE NG12 recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer for persistent unexplained hoarseness (or an unexplained neck lump) in those aged 45 and over — with no smoking requirement — and treating it with a spray/antibiotics without examination is the dangerous miss. Elicit and weight the associated red flags (a neck lump, unilateral referred otalgia with a normal ear, globus, dysphagia/odynophagia, sore throat) and the combined smoking + heavy-alcohol risk, examine the throat/oral cavity/neck/ears, and recognise an unexplained persistent neck lump as itself warranting urgent referral. Reassure genuinely (early laryngeal cancer is very treatable, often voice-preserving — urgent referral is precautionary) and address smoking and alcohol supportively without a lecture that alienates. The hidden agenda is avoidance masking a noticed neck lump and an unvoiced cancer fear (and worry about voice/livelihood and being told to stop smoking/drinking); gently challenge the minimisation, name the concern honestly while reassuring, and refer.

knowledge.summary: Persistent, progressive hoarseness in a 63-year-old heavy smoker and drinker, now with a neck lump and one-sided ear ache, meets the NICE NG12 criteria for a suspected laryngeal cancer referral. Refer today; do not prescribe a spray or antibiotics.

points.t: NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (appointment within 2 weeks) for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness or an unexplained lump in the neck. He meets both.

Referred ear pain with a normal ear, a feeling of something in the throat, painful or difficult swallowing, a persistent sore throat, a neck lump, weight loss, and stridor or breathlessness (which needs same-day assessment). Smoking and alcohol together multiply the risk of head and neck cancer.
NICE NG12: consider an urgent chest X-ray in people aged 40 and over with persistent cervical lymphadenopathy. Many head and neck pathways also request one; follow the local referral form.
Examine the mouth, throat, neck nodes and ears in person. The larynx is seen by nasendoscopy in the ENT clinic, so antibiotics or a spray without referral only delay diagnosis.

NICE NG209: give very brief advice and offer referral to stop smoking services; varenicline, cytisinicline (cytisine), combination nicotine replacement and nicotine-containing e-cigarettes are all options. Stopping improves treatment outcomes.
Use AUDIT-C or AUDIT to quantify drinking and give a brief intervention (NICE PH24). If he may be dependent, advise him not to stop suddenly and plan assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115).

Work as a publican, smoking and alcohol quantified, fear of losing his voice and income.
In-person examination of mouth, throat, neck nodes and ears; chest X-ray; nasendoscopy via ENT.
Laryngeal or other head and neck cancer versus reflux, vocal strain, infection; tested the "cold" explanation.
Asked about globus, otalgia, swallowing, stridor, breathlessness and neck lumps.
Stated persistent hoarseness with a neck lump in a smoker as needing urgent exclusion of cancer.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral today per NICE NG12; no antibiotics or spray.
Very brief advice and stop smoking referral (NICE NG209); alcohol brief intervention and withdrawal safety (NICE CG115).
999 for stridor or inability to swallow; chase if no appointment within a week; teach-back; review this week.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the pause about the neck lump and "I know you’ll tell me to pack in", and followed both.
Idea (smoker’s throat or lingering cold), concern (cancer like his regular, voice, a lecture), expectation (spray or antibiotics).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Your voice for work. Underneath (only if asked): your mate's throat cancer — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Calladine, thanks for joining. I can hear the huskiness. Tell me about your voice.

It’s gone all gravelly, weeks now. I run a pub and I smoke, so it’s probably just a smoker’s throat, or a cold that never went. Can you give me a spray or some antibiotics? I can’t be without my voice behind the bar.
Your voice is your livelihood, so I understand you want it fixed. I’d like to ask a few questions first so I pick the right thing. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges his priority and sets the agenda

model.text: Fire away.
How long exactly, and is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
Six weeks or so. Getting worse, if anything.
Did it start with a cold: sore throat, runny nose, temperature?
Not really. It just crept up.
Any feeling of something stuck in your throat, pain on swallowing, or ache in one ear?
Feels like something’s there. And my throat and right ear ache a bit, same side.
Any trouble swallowing food, noisy breathing, or getting short of breath?
No, I can eat fine. Breathing’s okay.
You said you smoke. How much? And how much do you drink in a typical week?
Forty a day. Drink, more than I should. Comes with the job.
Have you noticed any lumps in your neck?
model.why: Asks directly about a neck lump

model.text: (pause) There’s a small one. On the right. I’ve been leaving it.
Thank you for telling me. I get the feeling that lump has been on your mind. What have you been thinking it might be?
One of my regulars had throat cancer. Lost his voice. I’ve been trying not to think about it. And I know you’ll tell me to pack in the fags and the drink.
That sounds like a lot to carry on your own, especially after seeing what happened to him. I’m glad you’ve said it. I’m not here to lecture you. Let’s deal with the voice first.
model.why: Validates the fear and defuses the expected lecture

model.text: I’ll be straight with you. A voice that’s been hoarse for six weeks and getting worse, with a lump on the same side and ear ache, in someone who smokes and drinks, is something I must have checked urgently to rule out a cancer of the voice box or throat. A spray or antibiotics won’t help that and would only delay things.
model.why: Names the concern honestly, applies the NICE NG12 criterion

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I can’t tell without a proper look, and there are other causes. What I can tell you is that when these are caught early they are very treatable, and treatment often keeps the voice. Getting seen quickly is what gives you the best chance.
model.why: Balances honesty with realistic hope, links to his livelihood

model.text: So I’m referring you today on the urgent pathway to the ear, nose and throat team, to be seen within two weeks. They’ll look at your voice box with a thin camera through the nose, which takes a few minutes in clinic, and examine the lump. I’d also like you to come in this week so I can examine your neck, mouth and ears, and I’ll arrange a chest X-ray.
model.why: Suspected cancer referral, examination and chest X-ray

model.text: Right. That’s quick.

About the smoking and drinking: I’m not going to lecture you. They’re the biggest things affecting your throat, and cutting down helps whatever the result. When you’re ready, I can refer you to the stop smoking service, and we can look at the drinking together. If you drink every day, please don’t stop suddenly without talking to me first.
model.why: Brief intervention on smoking and alcohol, withdrawal safety

model.text: I might try the smoking. The drink, one thing at a time.
That’s a fair start. I’ll make the stop smoking referral today.
model.why: Respects his pace and agrees one step

model.text: If you get any noisy breathing, struggle to breathe, or can’t swallow, call 999 or go to A&E. If the lump grows, or you haven’t heard about the appointment within a week, ring us. Can you tell me the plan so I know I’ve explained it well?
Urgent ENT, camera up the nose, come in this week for you to check my neck, chest X-ray, stop smoking referral. Breathing trouble, 999.
That’s it. I’ll see you this week, and I’ll check the referral has gone through.

social.t: As a publican his voice and his work environment matter. Acknowledge the worry about income and work, and plan around appointments.
Alcohol is part of his working day. Explore without judgement and offer help at his pace.

legal.t: If alcohol misuse or dependence is diagnosed, he must notify the DVLA and should not drive until the DVLA has decided on his licence (DVLA assessing fitness to drive). Raise it only if dependence is confirmed, and document the advice.

professional.t: Track the suspected cancer referral and the chest X-ray. Document the red flags, the NICE NG12 criterion met, and his agreement.
GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: be honest about the possibility of cancer while giving information at a pace he can manage.

community.t: NHS stop smoking services, local alcohol services, Macmillan Cancer Support, and the Mouth Cancer Foundation for information on head and neck cancer.

redFlags: Hoarseness for more than 3 weeks, progressive, in a smoker over 45
Neck lump; referred ear pain with a normal ear; globus; painful or difficult swallowing
Stridor, breathlessness or inability to swallow (same-day)
psychosocial: Voice and income as a publican
Smoking 40 a day and heavy alcohol use
Fear rooted in a regular’s throat cancer; expecting a lecture
ice: Idea: "a smoker’s throat or a cold that never went"
Concern: throat cancer and losing his voice; being told off about smoking and drinking

playbook.diagnosis: Six weeks of progressive hoarseness with a right-sided neck lump, globus and referred right ear pain in a 63-year-old heavy smoker and drinker: suspected laryngeal or other head and neck cancer, meeting the NICE NG12 criteria for a suspected cancer pathway referral.
playbook.diagnosisLay: "When a voice stays hoarse for weeks and there’s a lump in the neck, we need to look at the voice box to make sure there’s no cancer there. If there is, catching it early usually means it can be treated well, often keeping the voice."

management.reflectIce: "You’ve been worried since your regular was ill, and you need your voice for work. Getting it looked at quickly is the best way to protect both."
management.psychosocial: No lecture: acknowledge the fear, agree one step he chooses (the stop smoking referral), and keep the door open on alcohol.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT today (NICE NG12); nasendoscopy in clinic
In-person examination this week of mouth, throat, neck and ears; chest X-ray
Stop smoking referral (NICE NG209); alcohol brief intervention (NICE PH24); do not stop drinking suddenly if dependent (NICE CG115)
safetyNet: Noisy breathing, breathlessness or inability to swallow: 999 or A&E
Ring if no appointment within a week or the lump grows; review this week

pitfalls.intro: This station is a head and neck cancer referral hidden behind a request for antibiotics. Candidates fail by treating the voice, not finding the lump, or lecturing a man who is already frightened.

items.fail: Prescribing antibiotics or a throat spray and reviewing in two weeks.
items.why: "Management not in line with current UK best practice." NICE NG12 refers persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45 and over on the suspected cancer pathway.
items.fix: "A spray won’t fix this. I’m referring you today to be seen within two weeks."

items.fail: Never asking about neck lumps or ear pain.
items.why: "Did not gather key red-flag information." The neck lump is an NICE NG12 criterion in its own right.
items.fix: Ask directly: "Have you noticed any lumps in your neck?" and about one-sided ear ache.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking completely, starting today.
items.why: Sudden cessation in dependent drinkers risks withdrawal; NICE CG115 advises planned, assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: "If you drink every day, don’t stop suddenly. Let’s plan it together."

items.fail: Opening with a lecture about 40 a day and heavy drinking.
items.why: "Judgemental approach." He expected a lecture, and it confirms his reason to avoid care.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear first, then offer help with one step he chooses.

items.fail: Missing the pause before he mentions the lump and his regular’s cancer.
items.why: "Did not respond to cues." The hidden fear is what will stop him attending.
items.fix: "That lump has been on your mind. What have you been thinking it might be?"

items.why: Stridor or inability to swallow needs emergency care, and missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: "Noisy breathing, struggling to breathe or can’t swallow: 999."

items.fail: Ending with "the hospital will send you a letter".
items.why: A referral without a lost-appointment safety-net leaves a gap.
items.fix: "If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us. I’ll check it has gone through."

timeMap.d: He offers "smoker’s throat" and asks for antibiotics. Acknowledge that his voice is his living.
Duration, progression, no cold, globus, ear ache, swallowing, breathing, smoking and alcohol, then ask directly about neck lumps.
His regular’s throat cancer, fear for his voice and income, expecting a lecture.
Honest explanation; early cancers are very treatable. Suspected cancer referral today, in-person examination, chest X-ray, one agreed step on smoking.
999 for breathing or swallowing problems; chase a lost referral; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes antibiotics or a spray; accepts "smoker’s throat"; never asks about neck lumps or ear ache; no suspected cancer referral; lectures on smoking and drinking so he disengages.
wordPics.pass: Recognises persistent hoarseness in a smoker over 45 as an NICE NG12 referral; elicits the neck lump; refers on the suspected cancer pathway; mentions smoking and alcohol; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: tests his "cold" explanation; surfaces the fear rooted in his regular’s cancer; explains honestly with realistic hope for his voice; arranges examination and chest X-ray; negotiates one step on smoking without a lecture and warns about stopping alcohol suddenly; clear airway safety-net and teach-back.

avoid.dont: "Let’s try a course of antibiotics and see if it settles."
avoid.instead: "Six weeks of a worsening husky voice needs a specialist look, so I’m referring you urgently today."
avoid.why: Antibiotics for persistent hoarseness delay a cancer diagnosis and are not indicated.

avoid.dont: "You really need to stop smoking and drinking now."
avoid.instead: "They’re the biggest things affecting your throat. When you’re ready, I can help with either."
avoid.why: A lecture confirms what he feared and may stop him attending.

avoid.dont: "It’s probably nothing, but I’ll refer you to be safe."
avoid.instead: "This needs checking urgently to rule out cancer. If it is, caught early it’s very treatable."
avoid.why: False reassurance undermines his attendance; honest framing with hope works better.

Use AUDIT-C or AUDIT to quantify drinking and give a brief intervention (NICE PH24). If he may be dependent, advise him not to stop suddenly and plan assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged his voice as his livelihood before directing the history.
Work as a publican, smoking and alcohol quantified, fear of losing his voice and income.
Picked up the pause about the neck lump and "I know you’ll tell me to pack in", and followed both.
Idea (smoker’s throat or lingering cold), concern (cancer like his regular, voice, a lecture), expectation (spray or antibiotics).
In-person examination of mouth, throat, neck nodes and ears; chest X-ray; nasendoscopy via ENT.
Laryngeal or other head and neck cancer versus reflux, vocal strain, infection; tested the "cold" explanation.
Asked about globus, otalgia, swallowing, stridor, breathlessness and neck lumps.
Stated persistent hoarseness with a neck lump in a smoker as needing urgent exclusion of cancer.
Suspected cancer pathway referral today per NICE NG12; no antibiotics or spray.
Very brief advice and stop smoking referral (NICE NG209); alcohol brief intervention and withdrawal safety (NICE CG115).
999 for stridor or inability to swallow; chase if no appointment within a week; teach-back; review this week.

social.t: As a publican his voice and his work environment matter. Acknowledge the worry about income and work, and plan around appointments.
Alcohol is part of his working day. Explore without judgement and offer help at his pace.

legal.t: If alcohol misuse or dependence is diagnosed, he must notify the DVLA and should not drive until the DVLA has decided on his licence (DVLA assessing fitness to drive). Raise it only if dependence is confirmed, and document the advice.

professional.t: Track the suspected cancer referral and the chest X-ray. Document the red flags, the NICE NG12 criterion met, and his agreement.
GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: be honest about the possibility of cancer while giving information at a pace he can manage.

community.t: NHS stop smoking services, local alcohol services, Macmillan Cancer Support, and the Mouth Cancer Foundation for information on head and neck cancer.

Neck lump; referred ear pain with a normal ear; globus; painful or difficult swallowing
Stridor, breathlessness or inability to swallow (same-day)

Smoking 40 a day and heavy alcohol use

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Six weeks of progressive hoarseness with a right-sided neck lump, globus and referred right ear pain in a 63-year-old heavy smoker and drinker: suspected laryngeal or other head and neck cancer, meeting the NICE NG12 criteria for a suspected cancer pathway referral.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "When a voice stays hoarse for weeks and there’s a lump in the neck, we need to look at the voice box to make sure there’s no cancer there. If there is, catching it early usually means it can be treated well, often keeping the voice."

management.reflectIce: "You’ve been worried since your regular was ill, and you need your voice for work. Getting it looked at quickly is the best way to protect both."
management.psychosocial: No lecture: acknowledge the fear, agree one step he chooses (the stop smoking referral), and keep the door open on alcohol.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to ENT today (NICE NG12); nasendoscopy in clinic
In-person examination this week of mouth, throat, neck and ears; chest X-ray
Stop smoking referral (NICE NG209); alcohol brief intervention (NICE PH24); do not stop drinking suddenly if dependent (NICE CG115)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is a head and neck cancer referral hidden behind a request for antibiotics. Candidates fail by treating the voice, not finding the lump, or lecturing a man who is already frightened.

items.fail: Prescribing antibiotics or a throat spray and reviewing in two weeks.
items.why: "Management not in line with current UK best practice." NICE NG12 refers persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45 and over on the suspected cancer pathway.
items.fix: "A spray won’t fix this. I’m referring you today to be seen within two weeks."

items.fail: Never asking about neck lumps or ear pain.
items.why: "Did not gather key red-flag information." The neck lump is an NICE NG12 criterion in its own right.
items.fix: Ask directly: "Have you noticed any lumps in your neck?" and about one-sided ear ache.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking completely, starting today.
items.why: Sudden cessation in dependent drinkers risks withdrawal; NICE CG115 advises planned, assisted withdrawal.
items.fix: "If you drink every day, don’t stop suddenly. Let’s plan it together."

items.fail: Opening with a lecture about 40 a day and heavy drinking.
items.why: "Judgemental approach." He expected a lecture, and it confirms his reason to avoid care.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear first, then offer help with one step he chooses.

items.fail: Missing the pause before he mentions the lump and his regular’s cancer.
items.why: "Did not respond to cues." The hidden fear is what will stop him attending.
items.fix: "That lump has been on your mind. What have you been thinking it might be?"

items.why: Stridor or inability to swallow needs emergency care, and missing it is a safety failure.
items.fix: "Noisy breathing, struggling to breathe or can’t swallow: 999."

items.fail: Ending with "the hospital will send you a letter".
items.why: A referral without a lost-appointment safety-net leaves a gap.
items.fix: "If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us. I’ll check it has gone through."
